messages.subject: procD.lm and advanced.procD.lm
messages.subject_clean: procD.lm and advanced.procD.lm
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have a sample with three taxa (A, C, and H), each includes males and females.

Research Question 1: Is sex a meaningful predictor? [FYI, it is.]

I could address this with procD.lm or advanced.procD.lm. However, advanced.procD.lm has some nice additional outputs, specifically among-taxon pairwise values. So, I fit the following model:

advanced.procD.lm(coords ~ sex, ~ sex + taxon,

                              groups = ~taxon,

                              iter=999, data = procD.df)

My question is whether the pairwise comparisons, such as the Least Squares distance matrix below, are computed after controlling for sex.

           A          C          H
A 0.00000000 0.05273518 0.03432703
C 0.05273518 0.00000000 0.06199359
H 0.03432703 0.06199359 0.00000000

Research Question 2: Does the pattern of shape sexual dimorphism differ between the taxa?

I suspect it does for at least one taxon. I'm not sure if I should think of this as differing slopes from F to M, or in terms of varying intercepts. In any event, I fit the following model. I would like to know if it is correctly specified.

advanced.procD.lm(coords ~ sex + taxon, ~ sex * taxon,

                              groups = ~taxon*sex,

                              iter=999, data = procD.df)

Thanks very much for any help.

David

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

To answer your first question, yes, the way you have set up the advanced.procD.lm is the way to control for the effect of sex.

Your second question was addressed mostly correctly, as well.  However, I would encourage you to use trajectory.analysis instead of advanced.procD.lm.  The attempt with advanced.procD.lm has the correct model set-up.  However, your pairwise comparisons are not as good as they could be.  advanced.procD.lm provides what I like to call “first-order” contrasts in means; trajectory.analysis provides “second-order” contrasts.  Specifically, for your research question, trajectory.analysis would find the trajectories (vectors) between males and females in each taxon and then compare these differences.  Instead of differences in means, it a difference of differences between means.  Since sexual dimorphism is a difference, it seems this is what you really want to know.

The example with the plethodon data in the help file should show you how to set up the analysis, which is actually easier than using advanced.procD.lm.

Cheers!
Mike

Thanks again.

David

messages.subject_clean: TPS grids for mean shapes not warping correctly
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I had something pointed out to me about my mean shape TPS grids. It appears that the landmarks of the mean shapes I have plotted using plotReftoTarget for each my groups do not lie on corresponding points of their respective TPS grids

The attached file "group means 090217.jpg", shows clearly how the specimens to the left of the figure (River female and male) appear to have been plotted at different positions on their grids, relative to the specimens to the right of the figure (Reservoir female and male). A quick check scan through a few publications containing TPS grids, confirm that this is not normal.

If the landmarks of a mean shape don't lie at the same points of the grid, as the landmarks of the other mean shapes, does this mean the grids are not reflecting the complete shape transformations? If not, why could this be happening? Could it be a problem with my install of geomorph or am I doing something wrong when computing/plotting mean shapes on TPS grids?

Here's the code I used

mat <- matrix(c(1,2,3,4), 2)
layout(mat, widths=c(1,1), heights=c(1,1))# set the size of the rows and columns

ref=mshape(smeltshp.gpa$coords)

# create plot area, set margins and grid layout
mat <- matrix(c(1,2,3,4), 2)
par(mar=c(0, 0, 0, 0))
layout(mat, widths=c(1,1), heights=c(1,1))

# plot mean shapes
riv.f<-plotRefToTarget(mshape(smeltshp.gpa$coords),shpmean.riv.f, mag=5, method="TPS", links=wf)

Daniel,

I don’t understand your concern.  I don’t think we are doing anything special in geomorph that is done differently in tpsRegr.  I chased down one of the references I think you meant (Franssen 2011).  It is clear in his figure 4 that at 1x and 3x, the target landmarks are not in the same place.  He also chose to use both grids and vectors in different plots.  In the vector plots, rather than use the consensus configuration, he used one mean to map onto the other.  These are all consistent with plotRefToTarget options.

I’ll emphasize this again in a different way.  When using a magnification and the consensus configuration (overall mean) as the reference, the following is happening.  The transformation grid shows how shape changes as one moves from the origin (of the projection into tangent space, probably) in a direction toward the target shape.  At the target, one can visualize the shape change, but as you said, this might be subtle.  Using a magnification means continuing on this path, farther from the origin and past the target.  One is hypothesizing what the shape change would look like beyond the target, but to do that, a configuration that is NOT the target becomes the target.  There is simply no mathematical justification for increased deformation without a change in target points.  This does not make sense, and I would be shocked if tpsRegr does that.  (Maybe somebody who uses both tpsRegr and geomorph can verify.  I have not used tpsRegr for years and have a Mac, so I cannot verify this.)

One could hypothetically generate a grid with magnification and superimpose points for the target (like I did in the last example), without including points for the hypothetical target, which seems to achieve what you propose.  However, to me this is a mistake, especially if the magnification is much larger than 1x.  Alternatively, one could change the grid density.  Sometimes using more little squares rather than few large ones visually emphasizes the deformation more at 1x.

Anyway, either I am missing your point or a critical reviewer who would be inclined to question if the shape transformations were plotted correctly, expecting the points of the target to match up with the target of the magnified shape change, would be incorrect in their expectation.

I did not receive an attachment, so I might be missing what your were intending.

Mike

Daniel,

Miriam is correct. The confusion you are having is not with the algorithm or with what is plotted (which is correct), but in what it means versus what you thought these plots are for. The convention in GMM is to show the shape deformation of a target specimen. This is accomplished mathematically by a TPS mapping of points in the reference to the locations of the corresponding points in the target. Thus they ‘move’ in the plot because one has asked the function to show that target specimen, not the reference.

If you wanted to show the TPS grid but also show the reference landmark locations, simply change the option ‘useRefPts’ to useRefPts = TRUE.  Using Mike’s example from yesterday, add the following:

plotRefToTarget(ref,Y.gpa$coords[,,39], mag = 5)

points(ref, pch=19, col="blue", cex = 0.5)

points(Y.gpa$coords[,,39], pch=19, col="red", cex = 0.5)

plotRefToTarget(ref,Y.gpa$coords[,,39], mag = 5,useRefPts = TRUE)

points(ref, pch=19, col="blue", cex = 0.5)

points(Y.gpa$coords[,,39], pch=19, col="red", cex = 0.5)

Dean

Glad to help Daniel.

Just one last comment to leave you with though, this time on TPSRegr. I believe you have mis-interpreted what the plots in TPSRegr actually present.  TPSRegr, does, in fact, plot the landmark locations of the reference deformed into the target locations, and not the original reference landmark locations themselves. This is easy to see when one accentuates the grids by 3X or 10X (the 2 base options in that software): here the landmark points continue to move with the deformation grid. So conceptually, mathematically, and from a graphical stand-point, there is no difference between the defaults of the two software packages.

But, as I stated in my last post, should one wish to use the other points instead when using geomorph, simply change the option ‘useRefPts’.

Best,

Hi Dean

I think that I misunderstood what 'useRefpts' does.

What I wanted to do was what Mike explained was done for Fig 4 in Franssen et al (2011) - see attached pdf. I tried making the tps deformation grids, with one group as the reference (i.e. plotting river mean shape using reservoir mean shape as reference and vice versa) (see attached "stream ref.jpg).

This appears to have done it, but the landmarks in the left and right grids, still don't seem to have remained "pinned" to their respective positions on the grid, during the transformation. I've either done something wrong, I may not able to do what Franssen et al have done with Fig. 4 using geomorph, or the nature of the shape transformations of my samples, are the cause of this.

Mike explained that the "extrapolation" of the shape transformation beyond that of the grid when magnified, is why the landmarks don't sit in the same position of the grid on both sides. This was if the consensus is used as the reference configuration. But if I'm using the other means as the reference, and geomorph is producing the deformations in the same way as tpsRegr, why are my landmarks not pinned to the grid, as they are in Franssen's figure?

Thanks again for your patience. I am just trying different things, and hoping to understand why I'm seeing these shape transformations differently, to other published figures.

This is easy to see when one accentuates the grids by 3X or 10X (the 2 base options in that software): here the landmark points continue to move with the deformation grid. So conceptually, mathematically, and from a graphical stand-point, there is no difference between the defaults of the two software packages.

A[, 1, ] <- A[, 1, ] * -1

Bjarni,

Whether you calculate variance on Procrustes residuals projected into tangent space or all PC scores calculated from the same residuals makes no difference.  The variances are exactly the same.  If you are asking if you should use only one or a subset of available PCs, my response is don't do that.  There is no reason to do that.  The first PC, as a surrogate for shape, can miss important components of inter-specimen variation.  More importantly, if the first PC axis does not align well with population structure, you run the risk of making improper inferences.  For example, let’s say that the first PC just happens to be most associated with allometric variation in shape and the second PC with subpopulation variation.  If you use use first PC scores only, you miss the appropriate characterization of the population structure in your estimates.

Thus, use the Procrustes residuals or all PC scores from them, unless you are not interested in Fst values for shape but are interested in some other trait that you have arbitrarily assigned as the first PC of shape variation.

Cheers!
Mike

Bjarni,

This is a question I am less likely to give a good answer, as I do not fundamentally work in quantitative genetics or population genetics, but I’ll offer two routes to consider and let somebody else chime in if there is an ardent preference.

Procrustes variance is the sum of squared distances of observations from the mean, divided by degrees of freedom, irrespective of the number of dimensions of the tangent space.It can also be described as the trace of either a p x p covariance matrix or an n x n covariance matrix, where the former is found from the cross-products of variables and the latter from crossproducts of observations.  Either way, the trace is the same.

The reason these alternative explanations is important is because how does one generalize the concept of Fst, Qst, or Pst for multivariate data?  Let’s use Qst for simplicity. Bjarni,

I’ll add a few thoughts to what Mike suggested. First I will note though that the conundrum you are facing is directly analogous to the multivariate heritability issue faced some years ago in morphometrics, as I’ll explain below.

For univariate data Pst is found as:  s^2_b / ( s^2_b + 2h^2 s^2_w)

where the s^2_b is the between population variance, s^2_w is the within population variance, and h^2 is the heritability.

For the multivariate case, as Mike mentioned the variance components are now covariance matrices, and there are two obvious ways to obtain a scalar estimate of Pst. One way is to use take the trace of each of these first.  Here, one has the total SS between and the total SS within.  One can obtain these easily from a Procrustes anova.  Note then that one still requires an estimate of heritability, or without these one at least can use a range of possible values.

The alternative is to retain these as covariance matrices, perform the matrix computations, and then obtain the trace of the outcome. Like Mike I do not know if this will arrive at the same numerical value, but based on the multivariate heritability discussion some years ago, my suspicion is that they will not.

Now, the description of methods above is precisely that used in multivariate heritability back in the early 2000s. Monteiro and colleagues proposed using summed Procrustes distances to obtain SS, analogous to the Procrustes anova description above. Alternatively, Klingenberg proposed a full matrix approach, much like Mike and I mentioned (note: their joint paper in 2005 in Syst. Biol. describes the different perspectives and interpretations).  Some colleagues and I used both of these approaches in a 2006 empirical paper to compare them, and while estimates gave similar biological conclusions, there was more to be gained from the full multivariate approach in terms of understanding patterns of shape variation.

So given that discussion on multivariate heritability, I agree with Mike and am inclined to suggest you retain things using full multivariate covariance matrices until the end of the procedure. That requires obtaining the between- and within-group covariance matrices from the manova SSCP, and using these for Pst estimates. The one complication that remains then is the heritability estimate. To generalize the Pst equation above, it seems that this would be represented as a p x p diagonal matrix, with the h^2 found on the diagonal.

One final comment, I know of a paper that compared Fst and Pst where the latter were obtained from GM shape data (Leinonen et al 2006). However, they found Pst for the first PC and second PC of shape univariately, so I would not recommend their approach.

Leinonen, et. al. 2006. Contrasting patterns of body shape and neutral genetic divergence in marine and lake populations of threespine sticklebacks. J. Evol. Biol. 19: 1803–1812.

Good luck,

Dean

Dear All

I have a couple of basic questions. I am conducting an GM analysis using 3D landmarks and semilandamrks. I define  semilandmarks using the function define.sliders() and I used the fuction proc <- gpagen() in order to call the Procrustes adjusted coordinates and  save them to perform analyses in another sotfware. However, when I compared the consensus configuration without slinding or slinding using Procrustes distance and bending energy they appear quite similar (except when I used the Bending energy the consensus configuration looks different) and when I tried to save the proc$coords the same values appear for each specimen independently if I did not used the sliding or use the Procrustes distance or bending energy. So, I am confused if really I am sliding semilandmarks and how I proceed to saving the Procrustes coordinates (with the sliding semilandmarks). Here I attach some screenshots to show my example. In each figure appear the GPA in the R console and the Procrustes coordinates of the first individual (AL2001aUM2). For instance in Fig 1 (without sliding) and 3 (sliding using using Procrustes distance) the consensus configuration is similar and the Procrustes coordinates are the same. In Fig 2 (sliding using the Bending energy) the cosensus configuration is relatively different regarding Figs 1 and 3 but the Procrustes coordinates of the first specimen (AL2001aUM2)) are the same as in Fig 1 and Fig 2.

thanks so much for any suggestion and please excuse my long e-mail

1. x<-read.morphologika(file.choose())#call data

3.  proc <- gpagen(x$coords)#extracting the Procrustes coordinates
4. a<-(proc$coords)# assign to the object a the Procrustes coordinates

1. x<-read.morphologika(file.choose())#call data

3. gpagen(x$coords,a)# Using Procrustes Distance for sliding or gpagen(x$coords,a, ProcD=FALSE)#Using bending energy for sliding
